explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The text says Sennacherib, king of Assyria, "attacked and captured all the fortified cities of Judah." Not most of them, not the good ones. All. That's not a few cookies off the tray, that's the whole tray gone.

I get why "a few" feels safer, friend, but the text goes bigger. It says Sennacherib, king of Assyria, "attacked and captured all the fortified cities of Judah." Walls and all, every one of them. If the count was a few, this would be a much shorter story.

Oh, if only it were one, baker! But the text says "all the fortified cities of Judah" fell to Sennacherib, king of Assyria. That's a whole list getting crossed off. One city would be a bad week, and this was a whole lot worse than that.

Right on target, baker. The Rabshakeh, an Assyrian royal officer, is sent "to King Hezekiah at Jerusalem." Hezekiah is king of Judah, and Jerusalem is where he is. The army heads straight for the king's door.

Samaria does come up in this passage, friend, just later. The Rabshakeh mentions it while he's shouting, asking whether other gods delivered it from his hand. But the king of Assyria sends him out from Lachish to Hezekiah at Jerusalem. That's the address on this delivery.

Hebron isn't in this passage at all, baker. The text names the destination plainly: the Rabshakeh is sent to King Hezekiah at Jerusalem. Wrong turn, but I've baked at the wrong oven temperature plenty of times myself.

explanations.answer: What Hezekiah's confidence is based on
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The Rabshakeh opens with, "What is the basis of this confidence of yours?" He starts by poking at what Hezekiah is standing on. Everything else he says builds from that one question.

explanations.answer: How much silver Hezekiah can pay
explanations.explanation: No price tag in this message, friend. The Rabshakeh never asks about silver. He opens with, "What is the basis of this confidence of yours?" The first thing he goes after is what Hezekiah is trusting.

explanations.answer: When Hezekiah will open the gates
explanations.explanation: That's a good guess for an army at the door, baker, but he doesn't ask it. His message starts with, "What is the basis of this confidence of yours?" The question is about what Hezekiah is leaning on, and nothing about gates comes up.

That's the word, baker. The Rabshakeh says, "You claim to have a strategy and strength for war, but these are empty words." Notice that's his opinion of Hezekiah's plans. He's the one talking, and he's talking big.

Brave is a kind word, friend, and the Rabshakeh is not in a kind-word mood. He says, "You claim to have a strategy and strength for war, but these are empty words." Empty is the word he picks. He's not handing out compliments.

Wise would be a nice thing for an enemy officer to say, baker, and that's exactly why he doesn't say it. In his words, "these are empty words." He's trying to make Hezekiah's plans sound like nothing.
You got it, baker. The Rabshakeh says, "Look now, you are trusting in Egypt." He goes on to say that's what Pharaoh king of Egypt is to all who trust in him. Egypt is the name he puts on the table.
Babylon never comes up in this speech, friend. The Rabshakeh says, "Look now, you are trusting in Egypt." Keep your eyes on the south for this one.
Moab isn't mentioned in his speech, baker. The nation he names is Egypt: "Look now, you are trusting in Egypt." He even brings up Pharaoh, Egypt's king, by name.

explanations.answer: A splintered reed of a staff
explanations.explanation: That's his picture, baker. He calls Egypt "that splintered reed of a staff that will pierce the hand of anyone who leans on it." Picture grabbing a cane for support and it snaps in your palm. That's not a good morning.

explanations.answer: A crumbling wall with no gate
explanations.explanation: A wall is a good guess with the story set in a city, friend, but he reaches for something else. He says Egypt is "that splintered reed of a staff." It's something you lean on, and it hurts you when it breaks.

explanations.answer: A dry well with no water
explanations.explanation: A dry well makes a solid picture, baker, but it isn't his. The Rabshakeh calls Egypt "that splintered reed of a staff that will pierce the hand of anyone who leans on it." His picture is a staff that breaks and hurts the hand that leans on it.

True, baker. The Rabshakeh says Hezekiah removed the high places and altars, "saying to Judah and Jerusalem, ‘You must worship before this altar.’" That's how he tells it. He's using it to knock down the idea of trusting the LORD.

The text has him say it, friend. In his words, Hezekiah removed the high places and altars, "saying to Judah and Jerusalem, ‘You must worship before this altar.’" So according to the Rabshakeh, one altar is the instruction. The question asks what he says, and that's it.

explanations.answer: If they can put riders on them
explanations.explanation: That's the catch, baker. He says he'll give two thousand horses, "…if you can put riders on them!" That's a gift with a dare stuck on the end. He's saying Judah couldn't even find enough riders.

explanations.answer: If they pay silver for each one
explanations.explanation: No price per horse, friend. The Rabshakeh's offer comes with a different catch: "…if you can put riders on them!" Silver never enters the conversation.

explanations.answer: If they open the city gates first
explanations.explanation: Opening the gates isn't part of this offer, baker. His line is two thousand horses, "…if you can put riders on them!" The catch is about riders, and it's meant as a jab at Judah.

True, baker, that's what he claims. He says, "The LORD Himself said to me, ‘Go up against this land and destroy it.’" Notice that it's the Rabshakeh saying this about himself. He's using the LORD's name to push Judah around.

The text says he claims exactly that, friend. The Rabshakeh says, "The LORD Himself said to me, ‘Go up against this land and destroy it.’" It's his claim, and he makes it right to the officials' faces. So the answer is True.
Yes, baker. They say, "Do not speak to us in Hebrew in the hearing of the people on the wall." They want the talk kept between officials. Men were sitting up on that wall, listening.
Close, friend, but gate isn't the word. The officials ask him not to speak Hebrew "in the hearing of the people on the wall." Those are the people who could overhear.
No hill in this scene, baker. The request is, "Do not speak to us in Hebrew in the hearing of the people on the wall." It's the people sitting on the wall they're worried about.

I wish he'd gone along, baker, but the text says otherwise. The Rabshakeh answers, "Has my master sent me to speak these words only to you and your master, and not to the men sitting on the wall…" He doesn't switch languages. He turns the request down and goes bigger.

That's right, baker. The officials ask for Aramaic, and the Rabshakeh says no. He asks, "Has my master sent me to speak these words only to you and your master, and not to the men sitting on the wall…" He wants the wall to hear every word.
True, baker. The text says he "stood and called out loudly in Hebrew." That's the very language the officials asked him to avoid. And loud on top of it.
The text says the opposite, friend. The Rabshakeh "stood and called out loudly in Hebrew." That means Hebrew, and loud, so the people on the wall could hear him just fine.

explanations.answer: It won't be given to the king of Assyria
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The Rabshakeh says Hezekiah tells them, "The LORD will surely deliver us; this city will not be given into the hand of the king of Assyria." That's the Rabshakeh's report of Hezekiah's words, and he wants the people to stop listening.

Storehouses never come up, friend. The Rabshakeh quotes Hezekiah saying, "The LORD will surely deliver us; this city will not be given into the hand of the king of Assyria." The promise is about the city not being handed over.

explanations.answer: Its wells will never run dry
explanations.explanation: Nothing about wells in that line, baker. What he reports Hezekiah saying is, "The LORD will surely deliver us; this city will not be given into the hand of the king of Assyria." The topic is who ends up holding the city.

explanations.answer: To eat from his own vine and fig tree
explanations.explanation: That's his offer, baker. He says, "Make peace with me and come out to me. Then every one of you will eat from his own vine and his own fig tree, and drink water from his own cistern." It sounds cozy, and he's pitching it hard.

explanations.answer: To serve in the king of Assyria's army
explanations.explanation: No army enlistment in this pitch, friend. He says, "Then every one of you will eat from his own vine and his own fig tree, and drink water from his own cistern." It's a promise of a home and a drink.

explanations.answer: To take silver from the king's treasury
explanations.explanation: No treasury raid in this offer, baker. The Rabshakeh promises that every one of them "will eat from his own vine and his own fig tree, and drink water from his own cistern." He's pitching ordinary life, and silver isn't in it.
Careful, baker, the offer has a time limit. He says they'll have those things "until I come and take you away to a land like your own." So he's not promising they stay. He's promising they get taken.
Good catch, baker. The Rabshakeh says they'll have those things "until I come and take you away to a land like your own." The word "until" gives it away. In his plan, they're moved.
True, baker. After listing the gods, he asks, "How then can the LORD deliver Jerusalem from my hand?" That's his whole point. He puts the LORD in a list with the others.

He does ask it, friend. The text has him finish with, "How then can the LORD deliver Jerusalem from my hand?" That's the question he's been building to. He's lumping the LORD in with the gods of those other lands.
Yes, baker. The text says, "the people remained silent and did not answer a word." After all that shouting, nobody on the wall says anything back.
You'd think somebody would, friend. But the text says, "the people remained silent and did not answer a word." Nobody on the wall sent a single holler back.
The gates stay right where they are, baker. The text says, "the people remained silent and did not answer a word." Nothing is said and nothing is opened.
That's right, baker. The text says the people stayed silent "for Hezekiah had commanded, ‘Do not answer him.’" The people on the wall followed the king's order.
Ahaz isn't the king in this scene, friend. The text says the people were silent "for Hezekiah had commanded, ‘Do not answer him.’" Hezekiah is the king giving the order here.
Uzziah isn't named in this passage, baker. The one who gave the order is the king in this story: "Hezekiah had commanded, ‘Do not answer him.’" It's Hezekiah's word the people are keeping.
You got it, baker. The text says they "relayed to him the words of the Rabshakeh." They came in with their clothes torn and told the king everything they'd heard.

explanations.answer: Urge him to surrender the city
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that, friend. It says they "relayed to him the words of the Rabshakeh." They report what was said, and nothing about urging him to surrender.

explanations.answer: Beg him to send for Egypt
explanations.explanation: Egypt is the Rabshakeh's topic, baker, not theirs. The text says the three men "relayed to him the words of the Rabshakeh." They pass along his message and don't ask for anything.
